DEATH Or LORD Havernx.—Another of the links which connected the present political generation with the last has been broken by the death of Lord Hampton. Remote from the strife of parties and sale in the enjoyment of an agree- able sinecure, he bat been so little before the public far the set few years that his existence might have been forgotten by many men to whom be was more familiar under the name of Sir John Pakington if it had not been kept in view by the retrospective criticism so frequently bestowed on the circumstances under which he was appointed to the post of First Civil Service Commissioner. The death of Lord Hampton places that post with ita salary of £2,000 a year in the hands of Lord Beaconsfield. Lord Hampton had some I merry ancestor.. King Henry Vlll.—surely when that pious monarch was iv his cope—grantedthe John Pakington of that day the right to wear his hat in the Royal presence. • privilege which may have had some value in those rough days, but which no proper...led person could exercise with inward comfort in these polio times. Another John Faking- ton was a chum of Queen Elia.theth's—the lady who moron to have had no one partner, because she had so many. Me gentleman was allowed to live at Court in great splendour— which he was permitted to do at his own expense, we are reminded. lie was a fine fellow, and lived at a fine rate, but kept an eye to the main chance, for he married the widow of a rich London alderman, who however—though he wane big and handsome fellow, and nick-named -Lusty Pakington "—saw him out, and married two more husband& once lord and the last an earl. Another Sir John was such a "trump " that when in trouble for his Royalist effort, no one would swear against him. Such a family deserved en- nobling. although one might think the title Hampton" a little unsuited Inn Tory. One of the most remarkable teats of tbe late lord was that he ventured into the matrimonial stale three times, and on the last occasion with a widow. But then he hat beeei at the War Office and the Admiralty.

During the past fortnight the Wesleyan March Quarterly Meetings—the most important of the year—have been held in the various circuit. of Methodism in Great Britain and Ireland. Them circuits number 847: 712 in Great Britain and 135 in Ireland. In addition to the ordinary and routine business, there here been the recommendation of candidates for the ministry, the annual numerical returns of Church rnembers,and the invitations of ministers for the ensuing connexional year. At the last muses the Wesleyan mem- bership was as follows:—The total number of members in Great Britain. 377,61E2; in Irelande on trial for Church membership in Great Britain, 23,048. As forte the returns Cl present show there is sot likely to be any large increase in membership reported at the approaching conference. According to the provisions of the Wesleyan Poll Deed no minister can remain in an English circuit for more than three years consecutively, nor be stationed in the same tnwn for longer than six years, nor be re-appointed tot circuit in which he has laboured before the expiration of six rears from the dateof his removal. On an average 500 Wesleyan ministers annually cloange circuits. At the once' no Conference about 400 ministers trill change their ap- pointments who have been each three years in their pr.ent sphere of labour. The suitable adjustment of no many ministers—a work of great magnitude and complexity at all room—ls somewhat lessened by the practice which now extensively prevails of circuita inviting ministers, and ministers accepting invitations. In each case the sanction of the March quarterly meeting Is neoesaary to give effect to the laritation.

The contest in Mid-Clic:Lire was the hot one fought in this part of the country. Li., the Eastern and IVestern Divisions of the county, Mid-Cheshire haw decided to adhere to Tory representation. The battle was gallantly fought, and the contest was watched with interest from all parts of the kingdom. Since the creation of the division by the Re- form Act of 12137, Mid-Cifeshire has returned two Conaerva. Lives to Parliament. Co 1868, at the first election, the lion. Wilbraham Egerton and Mr. G. C. Legli were returned. The Ron. F. 13. Vi'arren was the Liberal candidtte,and die voting ttien was—Egerton, 3,071; Legh, 3,037 ; Warren, 2,482. A vacancy occurred in 1872 by the death of Mr. G. C. lxgh, and a contest resulted, the Liberal ossididate being Mr. Li. W. Latham, and the COANII.LiVe nominee Colonel Egerton Leigh. The latter was returned by a majority of 1,3910 votes, the 'lolling being Legh, 3,508, and Latham 2,118. In 1874 Mr. Egerton and Colonel Legh had a walk over and in 18713, on the drethof Colonel Legli, Mr. Piers Egerton-Warburton was elected in his stead without opposition. Though the division was regarded as a stronghold of Toryism, gua,ded by vigilant landlord influence, die Liberals—imving a more perfect organisation Roan in the past, and counting upon a change hawing conie were the minds of the farmers in the division—believed that with the apread of knowledge of the abaolute secrecy of the balloh they could, with two popular candidate, wrest the representation front the brine. In Mr. Latham and Mr. Asinitage they had the two beet candidates that could have been found. Mr. Latham, though a landowner hints,' f, being A well.known consistent advocate for the rights of tettant farmers. The plidges given to tl.e Liberal tandidates were such as to lead to hopes of success, but during the last few days of the contest land age Tits and others busily employed theiuselvea among the tenant farmers in the interests of the Conservative candidate% Mr. Egerton and Mr. ll'arburton, and something easouring ve.y much of the screw " was applied. The upshot was that the victory woo won by the Conservative,. The Liberal, however, hal the satisfaction of considerably reducing the Tory inajorlty, and of proving this great stronghold of Coneervatism, that Toryism is on the wane. The voting was : Egerton IC), 3,806: Warburton (C), 3.7f.03; Latham (Lo, 1,314; Annitsge (L), 3,247.

Though defeated, the Liberals have in FAR, Weat, as well an in Mid-Cheshire, uiuch to encourage them in the future. In the East it was decided only at the eleventh hour, and when the chances of success for the Liberals seemed nil, to give battle to the retiring members who sought re-election The fizla WAS a plucky one, and if there had been anything like an orgauiaition among the Liberals the majority which Messrs. Brooks and Leigh scored over the Liberal candidates would have been greatly reduced, if not altogether over- ridden. In West Cheshire, where the Tories have held undisturbed possession for half a century, the Liberal can- didate., Messrs. West and Crompton, who made • gallant fight, deinonstrated that with better electoral organimtiou. this division of the eountv, in spite of landlord influence, may he plucked froin the hands of the Conservatives. The contests in all the three diviaions, if they do nothing else, will spur the Liberals on to perfect their organisations, and like their friends M some of the lancashire divisions, rid themselves of Tory doniination. The defeat of the Liberals io !did-Cheshire, as well as iu the other divisions of the county, is for the most part to be attributed to the (cm of farmers that their votes under the ballot are not as secret as they actually are. Tenant- farmtrs are slow to rmlise reforms in English politics. Though a manly and sturdy clam in most eocial relations ' in politics they have been so long under the iron heel of landlord despotism, and by habit learned to be content to be the retainers and followers of the owners of the nod, that it seems difficult for them to understand that tue Ballot Act converted the farmer.' votes into a true franchise, and that their votre are not to be discovered as in the old days of open voting, when the agents of lords of the soil marched tenants to the electoral booth like sheep to the slaughter. lime, however, is on our side; and ere long county elecbes will recognise along with their bretheren in the boroughs that the ballot is by its absolute wormy a thorough probe- boom the voter. In other counti. of England this has abeady been recognised, and them is now abroad among the rural populations in those cousties a vigorous temper of political independence that must make its example felt in I places where Toryism is bolstered up by fear and habit. Though the divibions of Cheshire have elected to cling to their old traditions their representatives will be utterly helpless in atteropta to arrest the Liberal measures of reform that will be pressed forward by the Liberal tiovernment that is on the eve of coming into power. One of the earliest measures of reform that will be dealt with will be the improvement of the franchise in the countima and a great blow will be Mruck at the political power of landlordism, which arrogates to itself the right to control the political thoughts of tenants as well as the cultivation of farms. The change is coming, and it cannot come too spwedilv. In the days when the franchise in counties waa a free- hold one, as well an the land, the counti. of England were the strongholds of Liberalism. In those days the stronghold. of 'Foryism were in the boroughs, rotten and corrupted. Then, how came the change? In 1032, by a clause, known as the Chandos clause—a Tory-Liberal ineasure—the franchise wars extended' to copy-holders, leare-bolders, and tenants-at-will paying • rentol £.50 • year. Toryism was then losing its hold upon Ito boroughs, and the object of the scheme was to give great proprietors that hold over the couMies that was slipping through their fingers in the boroughs. Tenants-at-will had long been accustomed to render homage to owners of the soil, and when the franchim was conceded to them, without giving them r,rotection against unjust exactions on the part of the landlords, its exercise became in many cases a servi- tude, and it remains ea to this day. Ilad the ballot, which formod • part of the original Reform Bill of 1032, been pamed then instead of forte years afterwards, the cringing of teimnta and the despotism of landlords at election times woul 1 have been less common than they are to-day. Mut a change is coming. The franchise will me long be extended to residents in ,counties on the same tunic that it has been given to town populationa; and if only canvassing is pro- , hibited by statute we shall experience in Cheshire and othm counties • healthier political life.

THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, APRIL 17, 1880.

Lou along the line, from north to south, from east to west, the policy of the Beacousfield Government has been denounced. All the English, Welsh, and Irigh conatituencies have declared their verdicts, and the Scotch Universities and the votera in the distant constituency of Orkney and Shetland have now only to elect their representatives to complete the new House of Commons. Of the 0.43 members elected in the United Kingdom 411 are Literals and 034 Conner. tiers, thus showing a Liberal majority of 577. A more crushing response to Lo,d B..aconnfield's appeal to the country torn vote of confidence could hardly have been calculated upon by the moat sanguine of his political opponents. No Ministry ever met with Isuch general condemnation, andno Ministry other than that which is now in a state of parturition ever deserved such a sweeping censer°. A stronger Liberal element Las not existed sines 1832 than the one which will be found in the new House of Com- mons. When Mr. Gladstone und his party rode into , power in 1008 the Liberal majority wasthen accounted strong, but the Liberal majority of to-day exceeds by 58 that which existed in 1808. In this majority, how- ever, the Home Rulers are reckoned, as they will undoubtedly be usually found in accord with the Liberals on all general questions. But supposing the Home Rule votes are abstracted from the aggregate Liberal strength of 177, the bwon -.fide Liberals would still present an overwhelming front to the Oppositiou bench. The Home Rulers are ei in number, and if they on some particular question determined to stand aloof from the Liberal party in the House, the Liberals would consequently still have a majority of 117 ; and in the event of the Home Rulers throwing in their lot with the Conservatives, both Conserv., tiara and Home Rulers on united groups would be in a minority of 57. Such a combination, however, is hardly like to arise, because the Hume Rulers have been smitten so keenly on the cheek by Lord Beaceme• field and his party that they are not likely to forget it for some time become ; but however forgiving the Home Rulers may be, the uselessness of such a combination with the Testes, and their chances of getting from the Tories more kicks than half- pence, are sutlicieut to put ouch an alliance out of the range of possibilities. Mr. Purnell undoubtedly made a bid for an alliance which he suspects may furtler hi deeigns, but his following even upon the most liberal allowance will not exceed 25 of the Home Rulers, whilst the remaining 35 will ateuredly accept the wider and more moderate leadership of Mr. Shaw. Mr. Bartell may be counted upon to on.- atonally kick over the traces, but Mr. Shaw and his followert can in relied upon to join the Liberal majority in divisions upon great measures of Liberal legislation. Putting aside altogether Mr. Parnell and those of the Home Rehm who accept his leadership, the new Liberal Government will have at its back a elear majority of i.o. With a powerful following like this the Liberal Government which will shortly take the reins of power will be in a position to accomplish much useful legislation. There is much required to be done in the way of reform and the Government, being relieved from an anxiety that a small majority must have given rise to, will be free to devote itself to framing and putting forth such measures of domestic reform that the country has been yearning for whilst the Beacosefield Government have been playing at fireworks abroad, and neglecting legislation tending to national development and progress at home.

ISte RIC.. TEXPLE, Bone., G.C.L., dm., Co. Governor of Bombay, has .erifteed himself at the shrine of Jingoism, for, like Ilumpty Dumpty, he has had a great fall. Onee he was a Liberal ; then his administrative abilities met with the favour of thoee in the high places of Liberalism, and there was a prospect of the baronet, some day, gaining the object of his ambition—the highest commission in the diplo- matic semim. But in a moment of weakness he fell under the spell of the Magician of Hughenden ; he was fascinated by the pouips and vanities of Imperialism ; and, dazzled by the peaked leger- demain of the Jingo God, he has fallen with his idol. Sir Richard held the Governamhip of Bombay, but, being a man of ambition, he determined to play for higher stakes. Resigning the governorship Bombay, he calculated upon win- ing a seat in the Home of Commons for East Won mstershire, and upoa then being free to be put in the running for that lucrative diplomatic off., the Vice- royalty of India, when Lord Lytton should be anxious to be relieved. Lord Lytton has suddenly become anxious, now that his master, the Hughendon Magician, has lout caste with the electors of the United Kingdom. Sir Richard, however, is in a sorry plight. Ulm the dog in the fable that mourned the loss of a lump of beef in an effort to .eure the shadow of the joint, he is in sack-cloth and ashee over his departed greatness. To give spa salary of £12,018 a year, with a oommand of all the fitmkeydom of Bombay, aiad to be treated with con- tempt by an English censtituerey is trying enough to the strongest nerved amongst the Jingo., but to have, ia addition, the contumely of the Indian people flung after him without measure, and in the mmt scornful vein, is enough to snake Br Richard cry outagainst the prophets who deceived him into the idea that East Worcestershire was a safe seat and refuge for him. The ledunt dcli New., after review- ing Sir Richard's career as Governor of Bombay, de- clares that "a more abject and eervile worshipper of power dom mot breathe ; a more euntemptible champion of the rights of Englishmen it would be impossible to find." It is pointed out that he refused the citizens of Bombay the use of their own Town Hall, in which to protest against Beaconsfieldism, and that to give effect to this purpme they were indebted to the courtesy oft travelling showman. There is a signifi- ' cant intimation that there was "so dinner, no ad- ' dress, no lined street.," when Sir Richard left Bom- bay, and we may berelore surmise that there were ' aleo neither streaming eyes of sorrow nor broken hearts at the departui-e. If the Ituf.da Lady News faithfully repre.ntes the feeling pervading the resi- dents in Bombay, it is evident that Sir Richard is not wanted in that region, however much he may regret him saoriSea of Cl2olB yew. lie is veritably of

The procession moved along Moughland-road, Greenway- road, High-street, Bridge-wreet to Halton-road, and the route was lined with spectdors. We may inci- dentally remark that the fie.g at the commissioners' offices was boistwl half - mast, as a mark of leaped to deceased. In Halten.road the toolestrians left the procession, whilst the conveyances proceeded to Frodsham Church, where. large congregation had assemble', amongst when) were the Rev. J. J. Bryant, Messrs. W. Wright, JP., S. Fl. Chadwick, JP., S. Ilastchurst, R. H. Mouritt, Henry Limber, W. 11. Linaker, Charles E. Linaker, H. U. Linaker, Arthur Linaker, A. Lake, P. A. the, Thomas 11. Hitchin, W. Whittaker, and Richard Lea. The coffin WU covered with splendid crosses and wreaths of flowers. At the church gates the coffin was met by the Rev. H. It. Blogg, MA., vicar of Prodsham, and the Rev. Canon Barclay, MA., vicar of Runcorn. The proper sentences, the lesson, and the psalm were read ay the Vicar of Frodsham, and the burial service at the grave by the Rev. Canon Barclay. At the conclusion of the service a hymn woe sung at the grave by the Overton Church choir. Mr. 11. Handle, of Bridge-street, ! Runcorn, was the undertaker, and Mr. Samuel Yarwood, of the Royal Hotel livery stables, supplied the hearse and , mourning coaches. Al the Frodsham Parish Church, on Sunday morning, the Her. H. 13. Blogg preached from John Ilth chap. 11th verse "Our friend L.:11113 slecpeth," and made special reference to the death of Mr. Garrett. At the clout of the service, Mr. Thoinas Riley, the organist, played the Dead March in , And.

On Sunday, both at morning and evening services, the bells of the Runcorn Perish Church rang muffled peale se a mark of rmpect to the deceased, and the choristers wore black silk shoulder scarves over their surplices. At the morning service there was a very numerous congregation, many of whom wore complimentary mourning, and the members of the 7th C.R.V. were also present,. '" . .

The sermon was preached by the Rev. Canon Barclay, who took his text from I. Timothy vi. 12, "Fight the good fight of faith, lay hold on eternal life whereunto thou net al,o called, and heat professed a good profession before many witnesses." He said that day, which ought to be one of rejoicing, being the first Sunday after the Confirmation, was alaiha day on which many of them had looked with great sorrow. The sight of mourners in the church—and especially the presence of a large contingent of the Rifle Volunteers, who had assembled at a very short notice to pay that respect which everyone acknowledged to be due to their late commanding officer— sights like these reminded him of the loss which that church and parish had sustained by the decease of George Garrett. There was to him something very sad and selemn in the thought that the very first occasion on which they had donned their new uniform it had been to do honour to the memory cf him by , whose energy and exertions it had been procured. For ' many months past he had been looking forward ,to a special church parade, because he did not think it right or seemly that his corps should appear in Goofs Home es they would have done had they attended as usual hat December in shabby habiliment.. Yet he who took se much pains with everything that had to do with the Church and her services, who had thought it not right to offer unto God of that which cost hint nothing, and who upon that principle never stood up to road a portion of Gol's scripture in that lectern—over which then hung the sur- plice which know its owner no more—without carefully studying it before in order to ascertain for himself, and int- preen upon hi, hearers the true sense of God's inspired word; who never undertook a perminent and leading part in some hymn or antham without previously practising the music— he was only anxious that the corps which he commanded should pay Rind' iar respect to the eervices of the sanctuary by appearing in their very bast. And well could he con- ceive the pride Mei pleasure with which, hid he been per- mitted, he would have marched at their head that day, show- ing by hie example bow truly he felt the need of God'e blessing upon their patriotic endeavours in their country's service. How truly he felt that "except the Lord build the house, they laboured in vain that built it:" but it must be the Lord our strength who alone could tnake their bands to war, and their fingers to tight, whether in the temporal or spiritual conflict. And they, volunteers, felt, as feel they must if they had a spark of feeling in them, that they had keit an efficient commander, whose concilia- tory spirit, combined with firmness in maintaining discipline, whose cheery manner indicated the true kindnese of his heart and rendered him well fitted frrt rto command which he hail no lately assumed. His loss was more or lee, felt by everyone with whom he was connected, whether in social intercourse or in themore serious business of life. No wonder that the news of his death, in one sense o midden and un- looked for, had cast a gloom over the community. and that,, too, in spite of a Parliamentary election. There was scarcelY an institution or .ciety in the town which would not m. i' George Garratt's help. Ann lawyer, implicit confidence wag placed in him, and many a client would seek in tad, for that professional assistance which sound judgment and no mean abilities enabled him to render to those who Fought hie advice, in whom a local bench of magistrate. would miss a diligent, assiduous, and able clerk, who took pains to make himself acquainted with all the bearings and intrictcies of any difficult or important case which he knew to be coming before the court. To his value ae a commanding officer of their corps, they as volunteers could testify; whilst of the willing cheerfulness which not only as a lay leader and an amateur member of the church choir, but on many other occasions, lie was ever ready to give his services; he could not too warmly or toe gratefully speak. In the course of a long parochial experience he had rarely moan Oh one who so thoroughly throw his whole heart and spirit ittr, every- thing which he undertook. Indeed, he most conscientiously ehrunk from undertaking any office, the duties of which he felt himself unable satisfactorily to diacharge. When, on the rarer occasions on which for that reason he felt com- pelled to refuse a request preferrert by those whom he estimated or oral, one could not but feel additional respect for the man whose conscientiousness led him to say "No." when his heart would fain have said "'Foe." He asked tee their prayers in behalf of his widow, then sitting in desola- tion, and the fatherless children, too young to know their loss, and for hint, let them offer up for him in the words of Nehemiah, " Remember me, oh, my God, concerning this, and wipe not out of my good deeds that 1 have done tor the house of mv God and for the offices thereof." The remainder of the rev. gentleman's discourse was addre.ed to those , young persons who on the previous Friday had been con- ' iirmed,and was en exhortation to them to follow out the injunction in the words of the text, to "Fight the good tight of faith, and lay hold on eternal life." " '" '' • " . . .
At the close of the service as the congregation left Mr. Johnson the organ let, played the "Dead Marcb.”

VISIT OF CHANCELLOR ESPIN TO FRODSHAM. The triennial visitation of the Rev. Chancellor Eepin to the Frollsham Rural Deanery was made on Thursday morn- ing at the Old Parish Church of Overton, near Erodehim. The I.imny MO read by the Rev. Henry It. !Hogg, the Vicar of Frodsham.after which the Chancellor delivered his charge to the churchwardens and sidesmen, in the course of which he referred to the formation of a new diocese, that of Liver- pool, and said they would all, he thought, rejoice that their own connection with the ancient see of Chester was not broken. He believed there still !wind in some quarters an idea that the attendance of the churchwardens that dav to be admitted to their office was altogether unnecessary t and some even went to far as to say that a,tentlance was simply demanded for the sake of the visitation fees. He would re- mind them that a person elected to the office of church- warden or eidesman had no legal powers, and could not claim the privileges and immunities of his office, until he was duly admitted thereto by the ordinary or his officer. With respect to the visitation fees due from the parish to the ordinary, they were fixed by the two Archbishops and the Lord Chancellor of England under powers given by an Act of Parliament. The order named the sum of Ito. for visitation fees. The amount claimed in the diocese of Chester, however, stood, as it had for many years. at 12, two-thirds of the legal fee. Thew visitation fees formed a main portion I of the einoluments—he might say. the note diocesan emolu. ments whatever—that were rrerieot by their archdeacon cool they were eupplemented by a grant from the Ecclesias- tical Commissioners. That grant was a fixol sum, calculated on the supposition that all the visitation fees for the year would be received, and P. 0 adjusted an to make the total salary of the archdeacon (including all the visitation fees)! up to £3o)a year. It was the bounden duty of the wardens in every way to prevent and to extirpate the illegal practice of buying, selling, and letting pews in churches over which they had control—a practice which was only Ims odious' than the traffic in benefices. Indeed, the wardens who abet- ted the practice subjected themselvea to a criminal prosecu-, tion in the Consistory Court for each a f iolation of duty. They should viligantly resist the growth of those supposed rights of property in pews, which in past times had been so mischievous. After alone experience he felt bound to state that the free and unappropriated system was on the whole the one that commended itself to his judgment as practically the best. Throughout the diocese the churches which were test attended by the poorer parishioners and by the labour- ing and artisan classes were churches under this arrange- ment. lie did not advise them to effect eudden and total changes in the arrangement of their chortle., for in many cases there was little or no endowment. Still he was of opinion that there were cases where a bold policy of totally abolishing alike the letting and the appropriation' of pews would tend to a great aud sometimes to a rapid in- crease in the congregatien, and a greatly increased congregation would he found to supplythrough the offertory a larger revenue than could Inc obtained from a smaller number of pew rents. Ile would advise them to keep the free and unappropriated system before their eyes as a model and a standard to he worked up to. The chancellor urged them to devise regulations for improving the financial arrangements by appointing a financial committee, and asked those wardens who were managers of schools to do the best they could to obtain from the school funds a contrilm- tion towards the cost of diocesan inspection. The moral of the great political change which bad just occurred, and of other political changes which seemed at hand, was thin— never was it so important as now to give in their public elementary schmle a sound education based upon religion and staunch Church principles. Never was it so important as now that the Church of England shout! hold her own in this work. Yet their diocesan board of eilucation. which was answerable for the salaries of the two diocesan inspec- tors, which also helped struggling church schools and throughout the diocese. bad been almost swamped by the deficiency in its income. If every church school woold contribute a guinea or two, according to Italics. throughout the diocese. the funds of the board would be ample and the contributions might be entered in th. balance sheet of the schools that was presented to the Education Depart- ment Attire close, the wardens and sidesmen for 19 parishes were admitted to their offices in the usual form.

div.head: HEALTH OF ST. HELENS.
div.p: THE HEALTH OF ST. HELENS.

At the Health Committee, on Wednesday, the Medic* : Officer (Dr. McNichol) present.' hie annual report, 1111Cil was • very elaborate and comprehnudre one. He congrato- -1 bled the committee on the comparatively moderate rate of I mortality from which the town had suffered. During 1879 the return of the load registrars record 2,3d5 birth, and 1,=3 deatha as haring taken place within the borough. making a birth-rate of 41.13 and a death-rate of 21.44 per thousand per annum. By deducting the deaths from the births it M s.n that 1,132 persons have been added to the population during the peat Year. The natural increase to the population in 1876 woe 1.173 in 1677, 1a37 in 1878. 1.163; and in 1879, 1,132, showing a steady, but by no means increasing birth-rate. It was well known that , St. Helens lay over the coal meamares. Ilioagh bounded on the west, east, north, and south by the red sandstone forma- tions. That might be 'lmposed .to be an advantage as to the drainage of the district, but that adv.tage. if any, was lost to them by the fact that the sult.il woe chide of . clay, especially in the townships of Sutton and Parr. The . rain did not easily pa. away Dom those places. because it was not absorbed by the ground, and the .wets were few and far between. The bonmgh contained an area of 8,500 acres, which WWI a rei.rkable fact Liken in conoection with the population. It was doubtful if there were another town of 57,500 inhabitants covering to large an area as ten square miles. If the streets extended over the borough it wool,' be favountble to the Ireaith of the neoplc, the less dense the population to the area the bitter, but the Borough of Of, Helens might be dee:riled us a large rural .nitary district, with a straggling town in the cent,. The populatior I of Liver- pool and Manchester was thick upon the ground. and they were known to ',are a high rateof mortality. Notwithsmading the eXCelle of births over deaths. the populdion had been at a standetill for the last twelve months. That must be ex- plained by supposing that the want of trade had driven many from the town. The births were decreasing in num- ber,—in feet the o.,nres were exactly the same ne in 1870 and that in face 01 00 increasing population. The lath-rate had declined, steadily, from 47.52 in 1871, to 41.13 in 1979. The marriagne celebrated in St. Helen" were only 379 for the year, 1879 being 54 lene titan the nuniters 1878. The death rate compared favourably with that of 23 large towns. Seventeen of them including I.,nden, Liverpool, and Gl.gow, had a larger inert:di:, than St. Helens. Toe city of Dublin hod actually a mortality of 351 for every 1.000 of the population. St. Helens immessed the ads.ntage of honk; as well ASto urban district, a rural one, covering so large an ar. as 8,500 acres, the population was not to dense per acre, and therefore the atmasphere ought to be more adubrious, and that doubtless accounted for the moderate death rate. During the past decennium, the death rate had been moderate and steady, with two exceptions. In 1871 they had a severe visitation of small pOO,OO epidemic which raised the rate of naortality to 30S1 ,ind in 1874 scarlet fever mused the rate to raise to 31-63. If preventable diseases such as twenties, scailatina, do., could be kept away altogether, or within bounds. the mortality would not greatly vary or be excessive. The deaths from zymotic diseas. numbered 737 at against 3= in 1878; 228 in 11877, and 336 in 1878. The mortality from thin class of di.a.s toot higher than any year since 1874, since they had had the misfortune to stiffer front two opt- detnics. Fever of all kinds causel aide:ohs—of that num- ber typhus being answerable for two only—which might he taken one proof that they bad TIOI much overcrowding in their midst. Three were cases of simple continued fever, leaving 31 as typhoid, er enteric. Among the symotica measles were the most fatal of the year. It began in January, and continued until the third quther. Tbc raortality of the year due to thin disease was 141. It was not oeo.il to have two epidemics prevalent at the same time but last year sarlatina paid the town a visit in the early part, arni stayed duriog the whole of 1879, b.oming nmre virulent towards the end of the year, after the departure of the measles. Both these diseases were unnsually fatal, the deaths being Oct of proportion to the number of easee of sickness to teens the lattercould he ascertained. Many died the aecond or third day, proving the malignancy of the epidemic. The fatality of both those diseases was caused by the low temperature which prevailed during the year. which in the case of measles induced pneumonia and hronchitiai and in the scar- latina a:Lat. caused dropsy to supervene. Both of those we. tootle diseases bad passed imay from them, eo that they were in a comparatively healthy state in this early part of 1880. They, as umul, suffered from diarrhas, ittother towns did, yearly but it was hiss fatal than it had been for mote time. In 1878 there was a heavy mortality (1321 from diarrheen caused by the great heat and dryness of the autumn. The weather was cold and wet in 1879, and they I had registered only 52 cases during the whole ymr 31 of which omurrel during the third quarter. Croup was very fatal, causing 2.6 deaths, 20 of which took place in the first half of Biel year, which was exceptionally cold. Though ' net exempt from whooping cougb, erysipelaa, and the minor symotics, the deaths from those were fen. Since 1876 there had been a marked decrease in the frequency of cemsump- don cases. Lung disea.s caused 2130 deaths, being 32 more than the preceding yet,. This increased faLdity was doubt- less due to the exceptionally cold weather which prevailed over the greater part of the year. Evaporation was carried on Monty, and the soil and atmosphere were alwaye in a damp condition. The report, of which the above is an extract, was ordered to be printed.

Petty :sessions, on Monday, William Leagh, labourer, Broad- heath. was charged with cruelty to a horse at Broadheath, on , the 27th March. Inspector Harper. Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, prosecuted. The horse : belonged too icensed hawker staying at Broadheath. On the evening of the 27th March a watchman in the employ of the Bridgewater Trustees now Leigh and A number of others. The horse was grazing within a few yards of the fence ad- joining the high road. Leigh was behind the others. and was seen to stoop down, pick up a piece of brick or stone. and deliterately throw it at the poor animal. It struck it between the eyes, inflicting a wound about an inch and a half long. The blood ran down and dropped of the end of the nostrils. The horse when struck spun round. and had the stone hit it t little higher it would no doubt lave killed it. The owner of the horse. Jamro llohnes, and the watch- man, an elderly man named Bowett gave evidence in sup- port of the cose.—Defendant we. fined 20s. and costs lid,

ATTRAIETIM MURDER oeeianero RA A William Cowans. labourer, was indicted at the Durham assize, on Thursday, for the attempted murder of his wife and family, at Haswell, Durham. The prisoner got out of bed and attacked his wife with the rolling pin while she was asleep. On making her escape, the prisoner tamed his attack upon his children, and afterwards attempted to kill himself by potting his head in the fire. Mr. SWANWICH. in supporting the motion, mid he desired to read a letter written by a tenant farmer living near to them, who led been exceedingly useful in that election, but woo had Icer, obliged at the last moment to withdraw his help in consequence of ill.healtb. It was as follows: Brother electors,—lt gives me great pain that I ton to. privid from Owing amomrst you to-night and addressing ynu. I commenced farming in 1b57 upon as rough a plot of land any to be found M the chanty. It was let pre- vious to my taking it to ten different tenants, so you may fancy what I had to contend with for a start. The fields were of all shades and siz,s, from one acre upwards. I com- menced about it in good c numb eradicated all Mside fences, Mimi up all pita and ditches, except one pit in the centre of the land, which I left for watering cattle. New fen,en were taken from this pit ao that cattle front any arid on the farm could he supplied with water. I raised all new !knees to perfection, landlord finding quirks. I think I might venture to my I made It the model farm in Cheshire, and it still re- melon no, house and buildings excepted. I man became a member of the Cheshire Agricultural Society, and ob- tained avers] prizes for improvetnenta on the farm, and once I secured the Brat prize for the beat-cultivated farm in Cheshire under ISO acres. I held this farm eight year.. I spent two fortunes upon it, and all the farm inade in the time I held it. Now, brother electora I think! have said enough about the farm, which most of you know well ; if not, make innuiries, ant you will find what I have said to be correct. I keld the farm under the late Sir Arthur Anna), a good old Cheshire landlord, who would do any. thing Le could to further the interests of the tenantry. But, alas, he departed this life, and no more Astons were left to take his plum. My fann was wanted at once when the young new landlord came boo poswssion. I had to leave without one penny for compensation for my outlay and the eight years of my best days spent with hard labour. (Shame.) I thought I was settled for life) hot none of you know for how long you may los aettled, or your children who may succeed you. So let me, brother electors,.k you to send sach members to Parliament as are pledged to do their utrtmat to amend them lairs. (Cheers.) Tin), gentle- men are Latham and Armitage; no vote for them freely. Ti,. ballot is strictly secret. (Hear, hear.) Who could vote for the Tories after making an act like the Agricultural Holdings Act ? What it profes.es to give with the right hand it takes back with the left. . .

I wan tallow with a large farmer a few days ago, but three miles from where you now sit, upon the same subject. He told orb, held his farm under the new not. I sskel, "Is your landlord a Conservative F" The angwer was, "No, no; 0 true Liberal from birth." Again, brother elector, let me ask you to do) all you can to support Latham and Armi- tage in this contest. (Cheers.) Now is your time. You may never again have anch a chance in your lifetime. (Hear, hear.) One of the Conservative cmdiglatee Paid when at Lynam "the land was not theira, they were only trustees for it." True. Then once more let me ask you not to vote for the Conservatives, but vote ler Latham and Arnsitaee. Why? Because you have it he your own hands now to amend the laws, and make the Agricultural Holdings Act compulsory. which is easily done by sending an overwhelm- ing majority of Liberals to repreeent the ccuntieP, and torebut any measures brought forward front the House of Lords to , affect the land, which House you all know is chiefly com- posed of large landowners. (Hear, hear.) The resolution was passed almost unanimously, and the , meeting closed with evens of thanks to the Chairman.

Cams, M.P., in supporting the resolution, aid their enetnies in Mid-Cheshire had done , everything in their power to wrest one mat, and he hod been . perfectly amased at the statement they put forward calling . themselves "formers' friends." Mr. Latham and his friends put forward two or three points; and although Lord Ear- tingCn had mid they had not done much for the farmer, but would do if put in office, those gentlemen claimed to have done many thief,, for the British for mm. When the Liberal party were in office they did nothing for the farmer. In 1868 they claimed the sup- port of the I annere as their friends, and made many promisee. They talked as now that the ratepayer should have a say in the distribution of the money he was called upon to pay. He quite agreed with them that it was perfectly right and a proper thing. They came forwent with a promise in 1862, when they had a majority of 120 or 130, to establish county hoards, but, although they re- mained in ollice until 1373, they never fulfilled that pro- mise. (Applaum.) They brought in the measure once and then pat it on the shelf, and now they said, " If you'll re- tnm at now, we'll do what we promised in 11163." I Ap- plause.) The Conservatiues had brought forward many bills, which they had been unable to pass in consequence of the obetruction of the Home Rulers, encourag.gl by a great , number of English member., for the express purpose of pre- venting the Government passing measures, which it was thought would tell to their advantage. (Cheers.) Mr. Howard, •man of high standing, and for whibn he had great respect, had propounded a scheme by which the land vrould produce three times as much as forroerly, and the land- lord, would receive £100,(H0,000 a year more rent. If the landlord received additional rent the farmer would have to ' pay it, and he did not think that would hen great consolation r them. (Applause.) There had been some violent attacks n the Government with respect to thequestion of local taxa- -1 tion. There never was such a gm+, misrepresentation, as the continued action of the Liberal party had been to oppose I any measures proposed by the Government to relieve the taxpayer. It was a monstrous thing for the Liberal party to my they wanted to relieve them from their local burdens. ! (Hear, hear.) From 1868 to 1874, although they had an no. ormous majority they were repeatedly bringing in mamma to put on rate after rate, until they (the Conservatives) said, "We'll not allow you to pass another bill to pot a local Irate on the linant of land, until you come mitt a remedial measure, so that it shall not fallow him, but be distributed on other people.” (Cheers.) Although in a minolity, they struggled and prevented Acts being passed for that epecial mean, and that reason alone, so as not to put a greater burden on the ratepayer without any relief being offered him. He thought it was a mmt monstrous proposition for for the Liberal, to claim that they were the friends of the farmer. The Conservativm brought forward a special Mellellre to relieve the ratepayer and ton personal as well as landed property. From 1371 to 1874 they (the Liberals) never rained their finger to relieve the ratepayers from their rates: but lord Har ington and his party ail voted against their interests and if Mr. Latham had been in Parliament he would have done the same. Their promises were very good and fair, and it the electorn thought they could believe them it WAS all eight; but they knew they opposed the Conservative party when they proposed to relieve the ratepayer and spoke and voted against him. (Cheers.) As soon as the Conser- vative Government came into power nearly 2i millions of rates were taken from the ratepayer, and in 'doing that they were opposed through Hoick and thin by the liberal party —those who celled themmlyes the friends of the tenants rd land.—(Cheers.) They were aware that so far as cattle I diseases were concerned the only possible way to keep their flocks safe was to stamp out the disease, or, better then that, prevent it rnroing hi. That was exactly what the Govern- ment did, and 311 the gentlemen on the other side—their magniflyent friends—opposed them. Mr. Cross referred to the Agricultural Holdings Act, and charge, the Liheral party with setting class against class, and, he mid, Mr. Bright was at the bottom of it.—(Cheers.) Ile (Mr. Cross) and his colleague+ approved of the principle of compensation for un- exhausted improvements. In conclusion the right hon. gentleman defended the foreign policy of the (iovernment. which had, he said, brought peace to Europe instead of one great European war. THE MESE OF CAVENDISH.

There bas scarcely been an important period in English history during the last two or three hundred years in which the Cavendiebes. Dukes of Devonshire, of whom the present Marqu:s of Harlington is the heir and chief representative in the House of Comtnons, have not taken a distinguished part, and that on the Liberal shin. During all that time the Cavendiehes have been the steady advocates of popular ' fights, and have powerfully amisted to preserve not only those rights, hot the popularity of the English aristocracy. It is now generally admitted that Lord Hartington possesson eminent qualifications as a leader under a constitutional government ; And there seem+ to he no doubt that Le will soon, if not immediately, rise to the premiership. Though, if chosen Prime Minister, he will have altzined that great office sooner than any minist, except the younger Pitt, he has acquired a reputation for prudence and good temper which would probably reconcile the country to ro early an appointment. Certainly the position of the Liberal party seemed to be all but hopeleae when he wan first named as iM leader in the House of Common,. Since than time he hoe had to struggle with enormous difficultien, and the Liberal succeseee have !wen greatly aided by the uniform , prudence he has exhibiMd in discuesing the important questions that have come before hint Rut he is not • man of devouring ambition. He is one who can .wait his time, and he is not likely to accept the premiership except it be the general with of the country that he should do to. Amonget the great national services of the house of Cavendish, perhapa the greatest were those of the last Earl and first Duke of Devonshire, in risking his life and his fortune in resisting the tyranny of James 11. In spite of numeroun foes, he steadily opposed the plans of that tyrant, and he was one of the three dukes—Devonshire, Leeds, and (if we remember rightly) Kingston— who planned the mining of Notting- ham Castle, then the only strong place in the central parts et England. These three noblemen met in a small roadside inn on the borders of the three counties of York, l/erby, and Nottingham, and there projected that hold enterprise. For the next lift, years the Ca vendiehes were amongst the chief defendere of the House of Brunswick and the British eon- etitutim and they have lost nothing of that love of con- , stittgiona liberty which they showed in former time,. The temper and judgment of the Marqui+ of Harlington will ' probably assist in gradually. nettling Home Rule and other question, which require delicate and prudent handling, and yet unyielding firmness—Liverpool Men ury.

Mr. Swift. of St. Helens, appeared on behalf of the police, and Dr. Clmmins, M.P., barrister. of Liverpool (instructed bw Mr. Husband. of Widnes) defended. When the p.II closed, namely. five o'clock, a large crowd of people formed, and down to midnight they made a most dis- orderly riot in the town. They paraded the streets, and stopped at different places. They were apparently under the leadership of the defendant Mr. Hewitt, who seemed to have sole cor.trol over the.,, for when he gave one signal the crowd stopped in their march, and when he gave another they proceeded in the work of demolition. 'Fake, for example, the diatribe of Mr. Cross Co Lymni, reported in to-day's E.rannsen and Tones. Speaking of a remark of Mr. Howard, whom he " greatly respects,- upon • plan by which the produce of the land could be trebled, he saya "Whet if it seem, and the former paid more rent, would it be any consolation to him?" Here is a Cabinet Minister who, having been one in • Council which for six years has moulded c' mighty State'. decrees," shows igno- rance that would shooed disgrace a fourth standard boy in a Board School. A fair artnage of rent on land taken where li. hired or paid in kind is half the produce. toe Mr. cross believe that if the produce were trebled th, mon,y rent, pahl to the moat grasping of English landlord, would be trebled too, or that poor and highway rates, wiezes, would be at all increased in proportion ? He had the face to quote the Agricultural Holdings Act. 11,011 a small farm when it pmsed. which I had improved con,iderably, and srm in good spirits for a few days. till I recHv.d a for- mal note from the landlord contracting himself out of it. The reference to Mr. Bright and his efforts by extending ownership to increase the produce of the Lind i• 1,10,101 M the extreme. The party of which Mr. Cross in leader have blinded their eyes and harderned their hmrts with regard to the farmers from the year of free trade till now. They won't I see that the grower of food for rutin or beam on Sl.glish I soil is neither more nor less than • manufacturer, Who ens I ploys Men, manures, machine, node plant, to raise certain prodnets, on the rale of which be has to meet the competi- tion of the globe. lie sends his corn and cattle to • seaport, at whose quays ride the great sea menatera whom a few hundred tons of coal and • few tons of ice have made to hear amom the ocean fat cattle, dead meat, arid wheat as good as his own. often at a freight quite low as hie own. Vet lie cannot call his farm his own to occupy. It is for certain times in the ymr his landlord's happy hunting ground or the poacher's), and he dare not kill a hare or rabbit, though , it is robbing him of a dinner, in his own garden. He is the only manufacturer in the country that carries on his busi- nese in the strait waistcoat of covenants and tenantry at will, and under the risk of losing his trade machinery from the operation of an unjust law. Imagine a cotton spinner in a mill held on annual tenancy, and with the risk, if not certainty, of his erected machinea becoming, iront the hour his tenancy ceases, his landlord's property. Further, imagine bit mill a preserve for rz.ls--which Mr. Wood tells as in • pie are very savoury food—not one of which he may destroy, but which destroy a good deal of his produce, and think of the owner of his mill having still the "cheek" to call himulf "the spinser's friend.
